Outside are the dogs, the sorcerers, the sexually immoral, the murderers, the idolaters

'Dog' was an insult for the impure or the morally degraded; Deuteronomy 23:18 uses it for a male cult prostitute. Dogs were unclean scavengers (1 Kings 21:23-24). Paul turns the term on false teachers (Philippians 3:2). Jesus' saying about not giving holy things to dogs (Matthew 7:6) reflects the same usage.
In the Greek world 'dog' was a common insult for the shameless (the Cynic philosophers adopted it). Ancient cities placed cemeteries, refuse and the unclean outside the walls.

The vice list (compare 21:8) describes those excluded from the city — not that the wicked live next door in the new creation, but that they have no part in it. Some see the present tense as a call to repentance while there is time.
I am the Root and the Offspring of David

Isaiah 11:1, 10: a shoot from the stump of Jesse, the root of Jesse who stands as a banner for the peoples; Jeremiah 23:5 and 33:15 (a righteous Branch for David). Qumran texts expected the 'Branch of David' (4Q174 Florilegium; 4Q285). The Davidic messiah of Psalms of Solomon 17 is the son of David who purges Jerusalem.

Jesus is both the source ('root') and the descendant of David — before and after him — combining divine origin and messianic descent (compare Mark 12:35-37). It repeats the title of 5:5 and confirms that Israel's messianic hope is fulfilled in him.
The bright Morning Star

Balaam's oracle: a star shall come out of Jacob and a sceptre rise out of Israel (Numbers 24:17), read messianically at Qumran (Damascus Document 7:18-21; 4QTestimonia) and later in the name of the revolt leader Simon bar Kosiba, hailed as Bar Kokhba, 'son of the star' (AD 132-135). Isaiah 14:12 mocks the king of Babylon as the 'day star' fallen from heaven. Testament of Levi 18:3 says the messianic priest's star will rise in heaven like a king's.

The morning star (Venus, Greek Phōsphoros, Latin Lucifer) heralds the dawn. Venus was the divine ancestress of the Julian emperors, and Roman coinage and propaganda associated emperors with stars (the comet of Julius Caesar was hailed as his deified soul). The promise to Thyatira (2:28) offers the overcomer the morning star.
Christ is the dawn-star of the new day that ends the night of the old age; he is the true royal star, not Caesar. The image completes 2:28 and the Davidic theme of Numbers 24.
The Spirit and the bride say, 'Come!'… let the one who is thirsty come
Isaiah 55:1: come, everyone who thirsts, buy without money. Wisdom's invitation in Proverbs 9:1-6 and Sirach 24:19-21 calls the hungry to eat and drink.
In the liturgical setting where Revelation was read aloud, this verse may have formed a call-and-response, possibly leading into the Lord's Supper.

The first two 'Comes' are probably addressed to Christ (answering 'I am coming soon'); the third is an invitation to the thirsty to come and take the water of life freely. The church, empowered by the Spirit, prays for Christ's coming and invites the world to him in the same breath.
If anyone adds to them… if anyone takes away from the words of this book

Deuteronomy 4:2 and 12:32: do not add to or subtract from the commandments; Deuteronomy 29:20 calls down every curse written in the book on the covenant breaker. The Letter of Aristeas 310-311 records a curse on anyone revising the Greek translation of the Law; 1 Enoch 104:10-11 warns against altering the words.

Ancient treaties, wills, inscriptions and books often ended with curse formulas against tampering; copyists' changes were a known problem (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.30.1, complains about manuscripts altering 666 to 616).

The warning guards the prophecy as covenant word: distorting it through falsification or by twisting its message to suit compromise invites its plagues or loses its blessings. It is addressed to 'everyone who hears', i.e. the churches, and is a canonical seal on Revelation rather than on the whole Bible, though many have applied it more widely.
'Yes, I am coming soon.' Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!

The Greek prayer translates the Aramaic marana tha ('Our Lord, come!'), preserved untranslated in 1 Corinthians 16:22 and in the eucharistic prayer of the Didache (10:6). Its survival in Aramaic shows that the earliest Jewish-Christian communities in Palestine addressed Jesus as 'Lord' (mar) in prayer and longed for his coming.
Cities prepared for the parousia ('arrival') of an emperor with prayers, processions and acclamations; Christians reserved their longing for the coming of their true Lord.

Christ's last promise and the church's response form the final dialogue of the Bible. 'Amen' affirms the promise; 'Come, Lord Jesus' is the prayer of a church that wants his coming, not merely predicts it.
Partial preterists hear an expectation of Christ's imminent coming in judgment on the persecutors (fulfilled in the first century) that still models the church's prayer for his final return.

Full preterists see this prayer as answered in AD 70; critics respond that the church has always prayed it as a future hope, as in the Lord's Supper 'until he comes' (1 Corinthians 11:26); proponents reply that Paul wrote those words to a generation that expected the coming within its lifetime.
Futurists see the church's prayer for the personal, bodily return of Christ, which remains imminent.
Idealists see the perpetual longing of the church in every age for Christ's coming, experienced partially in worship and fully at the end.
Historicists hear the prayer of a church that has lived through the long history the book foretells, still awaiting its final chapter.
The grace of the Lord Jesus be with all the saints. Amen
Jewish letters and prayers commonly closed with blessings of peace and an Amen (compare Numbers 6:24-26).
Revelation is framed as a letter (1:4-5) to the seven churches; Paul's letters end with almost identical grace benedictions (e.g. 1 Corinthians 16:23; Galatians 6:18).
A book full of judgment ends with grace. The epistolary close reminds readers that Revelation was sent to real congregations, to be read and obeyed in worship.

Partial preterists (Gentry, Chilton, Mathison) see 22:1-5 as the consummation of the new covenant order begun in the first century and stress that the epilogue's time texts ('soon', 'near', 'do not seal') show that most of the book's judgments fell within its first readers' lifetime, while the final coming, resurrection and new creation remain future.

Full preterists (Russell, King, Preston) apply the epilogue's 'soon' to the entire book, so that Christ's coming, the new creation and the river of life became realities in AD 70. Critics, including partial preterists, regard this as outside the historic creeds because it denies a future bodily return and resurrection; proponents reply that the time texts allow no other conclusion.

Historicists read the epilogue as confirming a prophecy that began to be fulfilled 'soon' in John's day and continues through church history to the final consummation; 22:1-5 describes the eternal state.

Futurists see 22:1-5 as the eternal state after the millennium and read the time texts as stressing the certainty, suddenness and imminence of Christ's still-future return. They note that the unsealing of 22:10 reverses Daniel 12:4 because the last days began with Christ (Hebrews 1:2), not because every event must fall within one generation, and that the promised reward (22:12) belongs to the personal return the church has always awaited.

Idealists see the river and tree as God's life given to his people now in part and fully at the end, and the epilogue's urgency as applying to every generation in the inaugurated last days. Hendriksen and Beale stress that the closing blessings and warnings are addressed to 'everyone who hears' (22:18), so the book's call to faithful endurance binds every generation equally.
Eclectic commentators (Osborne, Keener) affirm both the first-century urgency of the epilogue for the seven churches and a still-future consummation, reading 'soon' as prophetic imminence.
Amillennialists see Eden restored in the new creation immediately after the single return of Christ, with the time texts expressing the already-not-yet of the last days.
Postmillennialists emphasise the healing of the nations and the river flowing outward as the long-term fruit of the gospel, consummated at Christ's return.

Dispensational premillennialists see the eternal state after the literal millennium and take the time texts as describing the sudden and imminent character of the coming, consistent with a pretribulational rapture that could occur at any moment.
How does 22:1-5 reverse Genesis 2-3? List each element that is restored.
What should 'soon' and 'the time is near' mean to us, given that Daniel was told to seal his prophecy? Compare the main interpretations.
Why does the Bible end with the prayer 'Come, Lord Jesus'? What does it mean to pray it today?
What is the purpose of the warning in 22:18-19 for the churches who first heard it?
How do the titles 'Root and Offspring of David' and 'bright Morning Star' summarise the book's portrait of Jesus?
Who wrote Revelation?

The author calls himself simply "John" four times (Revelation 1:1, 1:4, 1:9, 22:8): a servant, a brother and partner in tribulation, and a prophet among prophets (Revelation 22:9). He never claims to be an apostle, but writes with an authority that assumes the churches of Asia know exactly who he is. Unlike nearly every Jewish apocalypse, the book is not pseudonymous: it does not borrow the name of an ancient worthy such as Enoch, Ezra or Baruch.

The earliest tradition is strongly apostolic. Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 81, c. 155–160, written after time in Ephesus) names "John, one of the apostles of Christ" as the recipient of the revelation. Irenaeus (c. 180), who had known Polycarp of Smyrna, attributes it to John the Lord's disciple, as do the Muratorian fragment, Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Hippolytus and Origen. Arguments for the apostle: this early, geographically close testimony; a natural reading of an unexplained "John" writing to Asia, where tradition placed the apostle; and shared Johannine themes and vocabulary with the Gospel of John (Christ as the Word in Revelation 19:13 and John 1:1; the Lamb; "witness"; "overcoming"; living water; and the citation of Zechariah 12:10 as "pierced" in both Revelation 1:7 and John 19:37 using the same non-Septuagint Greek verb).

The main dissent began with Dionysius of Alexandria (mid-third century, preserved in Eusebius, Church History 7.25). He accepted the book as inspired but judged that its rough, Semitic Greek, its self-naming and its vocabulary differ so much from the Gospel and letters that a different John wrote it. Eusebius (Church History 3.39) suggested "John the elder", a figure he found in a fragment of Papias, noting reports of two tombs of John at Ephesus. Whether Papias meant two different Johns is itself disputed. Many modern critical scholars (Charles, Aune, Koester) hold that the author was an otherwise unknown early Christian prophet named John, perhaps a Palestinian Jewish believer who migrated to Asia. Many evangelical scholars (Thomas, Osborne, Mounce, Walvoord, Gentry) defend apostolic authorship; others (Beale, Bauckham) treat the question as open and note that the book's meaning does not depend on it. Defenders of the apostle answer the style argument by pointing to genre differences, deliberate Semitising Greek modelled on the prophets, and possible differences in the use of secretaries.
Self-designation
"John", servant, brother, prophet (Revelation 1:1, 1:9, 22:8-9)

When was it written? (disputed)

The date of Revelation is genuinely disputed, and the decision matters a great deal for preterist interpretation. Two main options exist, with a few minority proposals (a date under Vespasian, c. 69–79, or under Trajan).

The late date (c. 95–96, under Domitian) is the majority view among both critical and many evangelical scholars (Beale, Osborne, Mounce, Aune, Koester, Walvoord, Thomas). Its chief external pillar is Irenaeus (Against Heresies 5.30.3, preserved in Greek by Eusebius, Church History 3.18 and 5.8), who says the apocalyptic vision was seen not long ago, "almost in our own generation, towards the end of Domitian's reign." Victorinus of Pettau (c. 260) says John was condemned to the mines of Patmos by Domitian; Eusebius and Jerome follow. Internal arguments: the churches seem to have a history (Ephesus has left its first love; Sardis has a reputation now dead); Laodicea boasts of wealth, which fits the city's self-funded rebuilding after the earthquake of 60 (Tacitus, Annals 14.27); the church at Smyrna may not have existed in Paul's day (Polycarp, To the Philippians 11, is read this way); "Babylon" as a code name for Rome is attested in Jewish texts written after 70, when Rome, like Babylon, had destroyed the temple (4 Ezra, 2 Baruch, Sibylline Oracles 5); the Nero redivivus legend in Revelation 13 and 17 needed time to develop after 68; and the imperial cult flourished in Asia under Domitian, who was addressed in some circles as "lord and god" (Suetonius, Domitian 13), with a provincial temple to the Flavian emperors dedicated at Ephesus c. 89–90.

The early date (c. 64–68, under Nero, or 68–69 under Galba) is held by J. A. T. Robinson, Kenneth Gentry, David Chilton, Keith Mathison and other partial preterists, by full preterists, and by some earlier scholars (Westcott, Hort, Lightfoot). Arguments: Revelation 11:1-2 commands John to measure the temple and says the outer court will be trampled for 42 months, which reads naturally if the Jerusalem temple still stood; Revelation 17:9-11 says of seven kings that "five have fallen, one is", and counting from Julius Caesar or Augustus makes the sixth Nero (or Galba); the number 666 matches "Nero Caesar" written in Hebrew letters, with the variant 616 matching the Latin spelling; the book repeatedly says its events are "soon" and "near" (Revelation 1:1, 1:3, 22:10); and the absence of any mention of Jerusalem's fall is striking if it had already happened (late-date advocates reply that silence is expected if the book's concern is Rome and the churches of Asia rather than Jerusalem). Early-date advocates read Irenaeus' Greek as possibly meaning that John (not the vision) "was seen" (still alive) under Domitian, and note his known chronological slips; they also cite later traditions placing John's exile under Nero (the heading of the sixth-century Syriac version of Revelation, which the original Peshitta lacked; Arethas). Late-date advocates reply that the most natural subject of Irenaeus' verb is the vision, that Eusebius understood it so, that Revelation 11 is visionary and modelled on Ezekiel 40–48 rather than a sign of a standing building, and that the seven kings and 666 can be counted in several ways.

This study does not decide the question. Each chapter states how a pre-70 or post-70 setting shapes the readings.
Late date
c. 95–96, Domitian. Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.30.3; Victorinus; Eusebius. Majority of modern scholars.
Early date
c. 64–69, Nero/Galba. Revelation 11:1-2; 17:9-11; 666 = Nero; 'soon'. Robinson, Gentry, Chilton.
Irenaeus' key phrase
'It/he was seen ... towards the end of Domitian's reign' — subject disputed
Why it matters
A post-70 date makes a preterist reading of the book as forecasting Jerusalem's fall very difficult
Status
Disputed
Genre: apocalypse, prophecy and circular letter

Revelation identifies itself in three ways at once. It is an apokalypsis, an "unveiling" (Revelation 1:1), the word that later gave the whole genre its name. It is a "prophecy" (Revelation 1:3; 22:7, 10, 18-19), standing in the line of Israel's prophets, who addressed their own generation with God's word while also announcing what God would do. And it is a letter: Revelation 1:4-6 opens with a standard epistolary greeting ("John, to the seven churches ... grace and peace") and Revelation 22:21 closes with a benediction like Paul's letters. Chapters 2–3 contain seven smaller messages, but the whole book was meant to be read aloud in each church.

Each label shapes reading. As apocalypse, the book communicates through symbolic visions, so its pictures are to be interpreted rather than photographed: a Lamb with seven horns and seven eyes is a meaning, not a zoological description. As prophecy, it calls for response ("blessed are those who hear and keep") and claims divine authority. As a letter, it was intelligible and relevant to its first hearers in Ephesus, Smyrna and the rest, which every interpretive school acknowledges, even when they differ over how much of its content concerns events far beyond them. Richard Bauckham's formulation is widely quoted: Revelation is an apocalyptic prophecy in the form of a circular letter.
Apocalypse
Revelation 1:1 — symbolic visions mediated by an angel
Prophecy
Letter
Greeting Revelation 1:4-6; closing grace Revelation 22:21
Read aloud
Blessing on the one who reads aloud and on hearers (Revelation 1:3)
Jewish apocalyptic literature

Revelation belongs to a family of Jewish writings from roughly 250 BC to AD 150 that scholars call apocalypses. John J. Collins' influential definition describes them as revelatory narratives in which an otherworldly being mediates a disclosure to a human recipient about a transcendent reality, both temporal (final salvation) and spatial (a supernatural world).

The key relatives: Daniel 7–12 (second century BC in critical dating, sixth century BC in traditional dating), with its four beasts from the sea, the one like a son of man, the Ancient of Days, the "time, times and half a time" and the sealed book; 1 Enoch, a composite work (the Book of the Watchers, third century BC; the Animal Apocalypse and Apocalypse of Weeks, second century BC; the Similitudes, first century BC or AD, with its heavenly Son of Man seated on a throne of glory); 4 Ezra (2 Esdras 3–14) and 2 Baruch, both written c. AD 100 in response to Rome's destruction of the temple, both calling Rome "Babylon" and grieving over Zion; and others such as the Apocalypse of Abraham, Jubilees and the Qumran War Scroll.

Shared features: visions and heavenly journeys, angelic guides who interpret, throne-room scenes, symbolic animals for empires, numbered periods of history, cosmic upheaval, a final judgment, resurrection and a renewed creation, and a sharp contrast between the present evil age and the coming age. Distinctive features of Revelation: the author writes in his own name to real, named contemporary congregations; the book is to be left unsealed because the time is near (Revelation 22:10, reversing Daniel 12:4); the decisive victory has already been won by a slain Lamb (Revelation 5), so the climax lies partly in the past; and it calls itself prophecy rather than secret wisdom for a later age. Interpreters across all schools use these parallels, though they weigh them differently: idealists and preterists stress the genre's symbolic, contemporary focus, while futurists stress that Daniel's and John's visions concern real future events.
Beasts from the sea, Son of Man, 3½ times, sealed book
1 Enoch
Watchers, heavenly throne, Son of Man (Similitudes), animal symbolism
4 Ezra
c. AD 100; eagle vision of Rome; Messiah's reign of 400 years then new age
2 Baruch
c. AD 100; Zion destroyed; messianic era; twelve periods
Qumran
War Scroll (sons of light vs darkness); New Jerusalem texts; Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice (heavenly liturgy)
Revelation and the Old Testament

No New Testament book is more saturated with the Old Testament, yet Revelation never formally quotes it: there is no "as it is written". Instead John weaves phrases, images and patterns into his visions. Estimates of the number of allusions range from roughly 250 to over 600 depending on how strictly they are counted; many scholars cite about 500.

The heaviest debts are to Daniel (especially chapter 7: the beasts, the Son of Man, the Ancient of Days, the saints receiving the kingdom), Ezekiel (the throne-chariot of Ezekiel 1 behind Revelation 4; the eaten scroll of Ezekiel 2–3 behind Revelation 10; Gog and Magog of Ezekiel 38–39 behind Revelation 20; the measured temple and city of Ezekiel 40–48 behind Revelation 11 and 21–22; the river of Ezekiel 47 behind Revelation 22 — in fact the book follows Ezekiel's order surprisingly closely), Isaiah (the trisagion of Isaiah 6, new heavens and new earth of Isaiah 65–66, the fall of Babylon in Isaiah 13 and 21, the Servant), Zechariah (horsemen in Zechariah 1 and 6, lampstands and two olive trees in Zechariah 4, the pierced one in Zechariah 12), Exodus (the plagues behind trumpets and bowls, the Passover Lamb, the song of Moses, a kingdom of priests in Exodus 19:6, the tabernacle), Jeremiah 50–51 (the fall of Babylon), Psalm 2 (the Messiah ruling the nations with an iron rod), Joel, and Genesis 1–3 (tree of life, serpent, new creation).

Interpreters differ on how John uses these texts. Beale argues John interprets the Old Testament as being fulfilled in Christ and the church (a redemptive-historical approach); dispensational futurists such as Thomas and Walvoord hold that the original Old Testament referents, including national Israel, retain their literal force; preterists such as Chilton read the book as a covenant lawsuit modelled on prophetic oracles against unfaithful Jerusalem; idealists see the Old Testament patterns (exodus, exile, Babylon) as recurring types of the church's experience.
Formal quotations
None
Allusions
Roughly 250–600 depending on criteria; c. 500 often cited
Most-used books
Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Zechariah, Exodus, Psalms, Jeremiah
Ezekiel's sequence
Throne (1) → scroll eaten (2–3) → judgment → Gog (38–39) → temple/city (40–48)
The seven churches and their cities

The seven cities of Revelation 1:11 lie on a roughly circular route in the Roman province of Asia (western Turkey), in the order a messenger landing at Ephesus would naturally travel: north to Smyrna and Pergamum, then south-east through Thyatira, Sardis and Philadelphia to Laodicea. Ramsay suggested they were postal or district centres from which the message would spread to neighbouring churches (Colossae, Hierapolis, Troas, Magnesia and Tralles also had churches). Seven was chosen for its symbolism of completeness: the seven represent the whole church, as the refrain "what the Spirit says to the churches" shows.

W. M. Ramsay and Colin Hemer showed that many details in the letters echo local history, geography and civic pride. Some of these allusions are widely accepted (Sardis' acropolis taken by surprise, Laodicea's banking and wealth); others remain debated (Laodicea's eye salve, Smyrna's "crown").
Ephesus
Chief city of Asia, major harbour (silting up), Temple of Artemis (a wonder of the world), provincial temple of the Flavian emperors (c. 89–90); Paul spent over two years here (Acts 19)
Smyrna

Prosperous port 35 miles north; early loyalty to Rome (temple of Roma, 195 BC); won the right to a temple to Tiberius (AD 26); destroyed c. 600 BC and refounded ('died and lived'); Polycarp martyred here c. 155
Pergamum
Old Attalid capital on a high acropolis; first provincial temple to Augustus and Roma (29 BC); Great Altar of Zeus; sanctuary of Asclepius (serpent symbol); famous library and parchment
Thyatira
Smallest city but strongest guild life (dyers, bronze-smiths, wool, leather, potters); Lydia the purple-seller came from here (Acts 16:14); local god Tyrimnos/Apollo, 'son of Zeus'
Sardis

Ancient Lydian capital (Croesus); 'impregnable' acropolis captured by surprise by Cyrus (547 BC) and Antiochus III (c. 214 BC); devastated by earthquake AD 17 and rebuilt with Tiberius' aid; famous textile dyeing
Philadelphia
Founded by Attalus II 'Philadelphus' (brother-lover); gateway to Phrygia; repeatedly shaken after AD 17, people lived outside the city; renamed Neocaesarea in gratitude for imperial relief
Laodicea

Wealthy banking and textile centre (glossy black wool); medical school near the temple of Men Karou associated with eye remedies; rebuilt without imperial aid after the earthquake of 60 (Tacitus, Annals 14.27); water piped by aqueduct, arriving tepid and mineral-laden, between hot Hierapolis and cold Colossae
Rome, the imperial cult and persecution

Revelation was written to Christians living in cities whose civic identity was bound up with Rome. The province of Asia led the way in honouring emperors: Pergamum received the first provincial temple to Augustus and the goddess Roma (29 BC), Smyrna one to Tiberius (AD 26), and Ephesus one to the Flavian emperors (c. 89–90, often called the temple of Domitian). Emperor worship was not a separate religion but woven into festivals, games, coinage, public sacrifices, civic banquets and the patron deities of the trade guilds. A Christian who refused to eat meat offered to idols, to join guild feasts, or to honour the emperor's image could lose business, status and protection.

The scale of persecution behind Revelation is debated. Under Nero, Christians in Rome were executed cruelly after the fire of 64 (Tacitus, Annals 15.44), but there is no clear evidence that this extended to Asia. Later Christian writers (Melito of Sardis, Tertullian, Eusebius) present Domitian as a second Nero who persecuted the church; Dio Cassius (67.14) records his execution of his cousin Flavius Clemens and the exile of Domitilla for "atheism" and drifting into Jewish ways, which some read as Christianity. Many recent historians (Leonard Thompson, Steven Friesen) argue there was no empire-wide Domitianic persecution and that Revelation addresses sporadic local violence (Antipas, Revelation 2:13), denunciations before magistrates (as in Pliny's letter to Trajan, Letters 10.96, c. 112), conflict with local synagogues, and above all the subtle pressure to accommodate. Early-date interpreters stress Nero's persecution and the Jewish War (66–70) as the crisis in view; late-date interpreters stress Domitian, the imperial cult in Asia and coming conflict. Futurists hold that whatever the first-century setting, the book's major persecution scenes look ahead to a final world ruler; idealists see the pattern of empire demanding worship as recurring in every age.

Numbers, colours and gematria

Numbers in Revelation usually carry symbolic weight, and almost all interpreters agree on that, even when they also take some numbers literally. Futurists, especially dispensationalists, tend to read time periods (1,260 days, 42 months) and some quantities (the 1,000 years) at face value while acknowledging symbolism elsewhere; idealists and amillennialists read nearly all numbers symbolically; preterists tie the time periods to first-century events, some (Gentry) matching the 42 months closely to the Neronic persecution or the Jewish War, others treating them as symbols of a short, limited span.

Colours, likewise, signal meaning: white for victory, purity and resurrection life (Roman generals rode white horses in triumph); red for bloodshed and war; black for famine and mourning; "pale" (Greek chlōros, a sickly yellow-green) for death and decay; purple and scarlet for royal and commercial luxury, the clothing of the harlot city.

Gematria (Hebrew) or isopsephy (Greek) is the practice of adding the numerical values of letters, since the ancient alphabets doubled as numerals. It was common: a Pompeii graffito says "I love her whose number is 545", and the Sibylline Oracles (1.324-331) give the name Jesus (Iēsous) as 888. Revelation 13:18 invites the reader to "calculate" the number of the beast, 666. The best-known proposal, Nero Caesar in Hebrew letters (nrwn qsr) totalling 666, is strengthened by the ancient variant reading 616 (the Latin spelling without the final n), but it remains disputed: Irenaeus, who knew both readings, did not propose Nero; some scholars note that 666 is also the "triangular" number of 36 and the number for "beast" (thērion) written in Hebrew; historicists have proposed papal titles; futurists expect a future person; idealists stress 6 repeated as falling short of 7.
God's fullness (thrice-holy, Revelation 4:8); also the unholy trinity of dragon, beast and false prophet

Half of seven: a limited, broken time of trial (Daniel 7:25; 12:7) = 42 months = 1,260 days (a literal 3½ years for futurists and many preterists; 1,260 years for historicists; the church age for idealists)
The world and creation: four corners, four winds, four living creatures
One short of seven; the number of humanity created on day six; 666
Completeness and perfection (Genesis 1–2); some 54 uses in Revelation; seven churches, spirits, seals, trumpets, bowls
Fullness of power, often limited (ten days, ten horns, Daniel 7:7)
God's people: twelve tribes, twelve apostles; walls and gates of the new Jerusalem
Twelve plus twelve (Israel and church?) or the 24 priestly divisions (1 Chronicles 24)

12 × 12 × 1,000. Disputed: the whole people of God, symbolically complete (most amillennial, idealist and eclectic readers); the first-century Jewish-Christian remnant (many partial preterists); a literal number of Jewish believers in a future tribulation (dispensational futurists)
